title: Exploring Antitrust and Platform Power in Generative AI
venue: 1st Workshop on Generative AI and Law, co-located with the International Conference on Machine Learning
extended_summary:
This paper examines competition and market-power issues in generative AI, asking how control over data, talent, compute, infrastructure, and research can concentrate power in a small number of technology firms. Rather than evaluating a teaching intervention or educational AI system, the article is a legal and policy analysis of antitrust concerns in the generative AI stack.

The paper argues that leading technology companies benefit from vertical integration across the generative AI pipeline, including access to large datasets, proprietary infrastructures, specialized hardware, and capital-intensive model training. It also notes that these firms can leverage historical dominance in adjacent markets to gain an advantage in generative AI, making entry difficult for new competitors.

The context is the broader technology industry in the US and EU, with references to ongoing antitrust actions and the emerging EU AI Act. The main conclusion is that current market structures and regulation may reinforce rather than reduce concentration, and that more substantial empirical analysis of product and geographic markets will be needed to assess dominance and competition in generative AI.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/argumentative workshop paper in law and antitrust, not an empirical education study. It provides no experimental, correlational, or qualitative evidence about teacher-facing generative AI coaching or lesson-plan feedback in K-12 settings.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper has no direct impact evidence on K-12 teaching, student outcomes, or teacher practice. Its relevance is limited to broad governance and platform-power concerns, not measured educational impact.

finding.finding_summary: This paper is a legal/policy analysis of generative AI market concentration and antitrust issues, not an empirical study of educational outcomes or teacher-facing AI coaching. It does not report intervention effects, sample sizes, or quantitative outcome measures; instead, it argues that current GenAI markets are dominated by a few firms and that regulation may reinforce existing power structures.
finding.measure: Legal/policy analysis of market dominance, vertical integration, and regulatory implications
